title: CHEM1A Practice Quiz — Objective 3: Mole & Composition (DRAFT pending Gilley approval)

items.stem: What is the molar mass of MgCl₂? (Mg = 24.31, Cl = 35.45)
items.explain: 24.31 + 2(35.45) = 95.21 g/mol. Forgetting the subscript 2 gives 59.76; tripling the chlorine gives 130.66; 36 comes from adding atomic NUMBERS (12 + 17 + 17 ÷ 2?) — masses and numbers are different columns of the periodic table.

items.stem: What is the molar mass of (NH₄)₂S? (N = 14.01, H = 1.008, S = 32.07)
items.explain: The parentheses multiply everything inside by 2: 2(14.01) + 8(1.008) + 32.07 = 68.15 g/mol. 50.12 counts only one NH₄; the parentheses are the most common molar-mass slip.

items.stem: How many moles are in 9.01 g of water (H₂O, 18.02 g/mol)?
items.explain: 9.01 g × (1 mol / 18.02 g) = 0.500 mol. Dividing the other way gives 2.00 (inverted factor); treating grams as moles gives 9.01; multiplying gives 162. Units canceling tells you which way the factor goes.

items.stem: Equal 10.0 g samples of four substances — which contains the MOST molecules?
items.explain: Equal mass ÷ smallest molar mass = most moles = most molecules. Lighter molecules pack more particles into the same grams. Picking the heaviest molar mass inverts the reasoning.

items.stem: What is the mass percent of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂? (H = 1.008, O = 16.00; molar mass 34.02 g/mol)
items.explain: 2(16.00)/34.02 = 94.07%. 50% is the atom-count trap (2 of 4 atoms) — percent composition is by MASS; 5.93% is hydrogen's share.

items.stem: Which compound has the highest mass percent of nitrogen?
items.explain: NH₃: 14.01/17.03 = 82%. Hydrogen barely adds mass, so ammonia is almost all nitrogen by mass. NO = 47%, NO₂ = 30%, N₂O = 64%. Counting nitrogen atoms alone (which favors N₂O's two) is the misconception.

items.stem: A compound is 50.05% sulfur and 49.95% oxygen by mass. Its empirical formula is: (S = 32.07, O = 16.00)
items.explain: 50.05/32.07 = 1.561 mol S; 49.95/16.00 = 3.122 mol O → 1 : 2 → SO₂. Equal percents do NOT mean equal atoms — sulfur atoms are twice as heavy, so half as many.

items.stem: Which of these could be an empirical formula?
items.explain: An empirical formula is already in the smallest whole-number ratio. C₂H₆ reduces to CH₃, C₃H₆ to CH₂, H₂O₂ to HO — only CH₄O cannot be reduced.

items.stem: A compound has empirical formula C₂H₅ and molar mass 58.1 g/mol. Its molecular formula is:
items.explain: Empirical mass = 29.06 g/mol; n = 58.1/29.06 = 2 → multiply ALL subscripts by 2 → C₄H₁₀. C₂H₁₀ multiplies only the hydrogen — n scales the whole formula.

items.stem: To turn an empirical formula into a molecular formula, what single additional piece of information do you need?
choices: The molar mass of the compound
The number of moles in the sample
items.explain: n = molar mass ÷ empirical-formula mass, then multiply the subscripts by n. Percent composition only ever gives the ratio — it cannot distinguish C₂H₄ from C₆H₁₂.

items.stem: In combustion analysis of a carbon-hydrogen compound, the carbon in the sample is measured by weighing:
items.explain: Every carbon atom exits in exactly one CO₂ molecule, so mol CO₂ = mol C. The hydrogen is caught the same way as H₂O — with TWO hydrogens per water.

items.stem: Combustion of a hydrocarbon gives 0.200 mol of CO₂ and 0.300 mol of H₂O. The empirical formula is:
items.explain: mol C = 0.200; mol H = 0.300 × 2 = 0.600 → 1 : 3 → CH₃. Forgetting the 2 hydrogens per water gives C₂H₃; C₂H₆ is a molecular formula, not the smallest ratio.

items.stem: 0.250 mol of KBr is dissolved in enough water to make 500.0 mL of solution. The molarity is:
items.explain: 0.250 mol ÷ 0.5000 L = 0.500 M. Multiplying gives 0.125; dividing by milliliters gives 5.0 × 10⁻⁴; ignoring the volume leaves 0.250. Convert to liters first, every time.

items.stem: What is the nitrate ion concentration in a 0.25 M solution of Ca(NO₃)₂?
items.explain: Each formula unit releases TWO nitrate ions: 2 × 0.25 = 0.50 M. Reading the subscript as 3 (from NO₃) instead of the 2 outside the parentheses gives 0.75 — the subscript that multiplies is the one on the ion.

items.stem: 50.0 mL of a 2.00 M solution is diluted to a final volume of 200.0 mL. The new concentration is:
items.explain: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂: (2.00)(50.0) = M₂(200.0) → 0.500 M. Volume went up 4×, so concentration comes down 4×. Getting 8.00 M means the ratio was flipped — dilution can only decrease concentration.

items.stem: To prepare 100.0 mL of 0.100 M solution from a 1.00 M stock, you should:
choices: Measure 10.0 mL of stock, then add water up to the 100.0 mL mark
Add 100.0 mL of water to 10.0 mL of stock
Measure 90.0 mL of stock and 10.0 mL of water
Boil the stock down to one tenth of its volume
items.explain: V₁ = (0.100 × 100.0)/1.00 = 10.0 mL of stock, diluted TO a final volume of 100.0 mL. Adding 100.0 mL of water gives 110 mL total — 'dilute to' is a final volume, not an amount of water added.

items.stem: 5.0 g of salt is dissolved in 45.0 g of water. The mass percent of salt is:
items.explain: 5.0/(5.0 + 45.0) × 100 = 10.% — the denominator is the WHOLE solution. Dividing by the water alone (5.0/45.0 = 11%) is the classic mass-percent mistake.

items.stem: A water sample contains 3.5 mg of fluoride per kilogram of solution. Its fluoride concentration is:
items.explain: 1 mg per kg is 1 mg per 10⁶ mg — exactly one part per million. Parts per billion would be micrograms per kilogram; mass percent would be grams per hundred grams.

items.stem: The mole is best described as:
choices: A counting unit — the amount containing as many particles as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12
A unit of mass equal to the atomic mass
The volume occupied by a gas
The number of grams in one liter of solution
items.explain: The mole counts particles (6.022 × 10²³ of them), the way a dozen counts eggs. It is not itself a mass or a volume — molar mass and molar volume attach those separately.

items.stem: In a sugar-water solution, the water is the:
items.explain: The solvent is the component that does the dissolving — present in the greater amount. The sugar is the solute. Precipitates form when something comes OUT of solution.
